title: PolySHAP: Extending KernelSHAP with Interaction-Informed Polynomial Regression
claim: A baseline fits a linear surrogate to sampled game evaluations; ours fits a richer polynomial surrogate and still recovers attributions exactly.
layout: 3 columns left-to-right, two stacked parallel rows (baseline vs ours), block arrows
description: A three-stage left-to-right diagram in dashed rounded panels titled Sampling, a method column, and Extract SV. On the left, a tall red vector labeled Game v is sampled into subsets v(S1), v(S2), ..., v(Sm), which form a shorter red vector. Two parallel rows follow. The top KernelSHAP row shows a single green matrix approximately equal to a small blue-grey vector, with a mini plot of red points and a flat line labeled Linear approximation. The bottom PolySHAP row has a wider two-tone green matrix, labeled Interactions I, a darker blue vector, and a plot where a curved parabola fits the points, labeled Polynomial approximation. Block arrows lead to the right panel. It shows the SV symbol on top and a summation formula over T on the bottom. The eye goes first to the red vectors, then to the contrast between the flat line and the curve.
caption: Both KernelSHAP and PolySHAP fit a function to approximate a sample of game evaluations. While KernelSHAP uses a linear approximation, PolySHAP uses a more expressive polynomial approximation. Finally, both algorithms return the Shapley values (SV) of their respective approximations (trivial for KernelSHAP, see Theorem [ref] for PolySHAP).
abstract: Shapley values have emerged as a central game-theoretic tool in explainable AI (XAI). However, computing Shapley values exactly requires $2^d$ game evaluations for a model with $d$ features. Lundberg and Lee's KernelSHAP algorithm has emerged as a leading method for avoiding this exponential cost. KernelSHAP approximates Shapley values by approximating the game as a linear function, which is fit using a small number of game evaluations for random feature subsets. In this work, we extend KernelSHAP by approximating the game via higher degree polynomials, which capture non-linear interactions between features. Our resulting PolySHAP method yields empirically better Shapley value estimates for various benchmark datasets, and we prove that these estimates are consistent. Moreover, we connect our approach to paired sampling (antithetic sampling), a ubiquitous modification to KernelSHAP that improves empirical accuracy. We prove that paired sampling outputs exactly the same Shapley value approximations as second-order PolySHAP, without ever fitting a degree 2 polynomial. To the best of our knowledge, this finding provides the first strong theoretical justification for the excellent practical performance of the paired sampling heuristic.
